title: Heavy-command admission queue — capacity-aware throttle across dispatched lanes
summary: Prior-art survey for backlog #3456: as the mechanical dispatcher scales lane parallelism, nothing today caps how many genuinely CPU/IO-heavy commands (check:standards, verify-lane/test:unit, npm ci, a Playwright visual capture) may run at the same instant across independently-dispatched lane processes, even though each lane's own lease is valid. Surveys four axes against shipped prior art. Classification: Bazel's local-resource scheduler tracks a pool against a per-action declared cost, not a blanket per-job slot — precedent for an explicit, weighted command list over either a uniform cap or a not-yet-buildable adaptive classifier. Binding point: GNU Make's jobserver protocol acquires a token immediately before a job runs and releases it after, never at process-start time, with one implicit slot always reserved — precedent for gating at heavy-command-invocation time, not lane-acquire time, keeping lane leasing and CPU capacity genuinely decoupled. Cap shape: Bazel's own default pool is a measured-once host fact, not continuously resampled; GNU Parallel's --load — real shipped adaptive throttling — deliberately avoids raw os.loadavg() (too slow) in favor of a dedicated instantaneous ps-based signal, showing adaptive throttling is a nontrivial, currently-absent measurement layer, not a drop-in swap for a fixed constant. Surfacing: GitHub Actions concurrency groups expose a queued job as a first-class visible state, never silence. A fifth finding: this repo already ships two independently-designed cross-process single-holder mutexes (scripts/readiness/file-locks.mjs's heartbeat-TTL lock dir, scripts/conveyor/infra-blocked.mjs's withInfraLock) that are the natural generalization target from N=1 to N=cap, once a mechanism is chosen.
